description: Set, lighting, sound and costume choices that move between Japanese coast and North Korean compound.
content_html:
Two Worlds on One Stage

The design challenge of The Great Wave is fundamental: how do you put Japan and North Korea on the same stage without either location feeling vague? Turnly’s play demands a design language that can differentiate between two politically and emotionally distinct worlds, often within the same scene transition. The solution most productions reach for is not naturalistic scene-painting but a split staging strategy: a stage divided so that the Japanese household and the North Korean compound can each claim a permanent location, with lighting doing the work of telling the audience where they are.

For a staging configuration, an end-on or thrust stage both offer advantages for this play. A thrust configuration brings the audience close to both worlds simultaneously, collapsing any comfortable distance between spectator and the injustice they are watching — a Brechtian effect even in a predominantly naturalistic production.

Key Fact

The two locations demand contrasting design vocabularies: Japan evokes domestic warmth and coastal openness — natural light, timber, the blue-grey of the sea. North Korea evokes state control — flat, harsh overhead light, institutional walls, the absence of the natural world. Every design choice should be readable as belonging to one or the other.

Lighting Design: From Coastal Softness to State Searchlight

The Japan scenes can be lit with a warm amber-tinted lighting wash that evokes domestic interior light and coastal afternoon. For the North Korean compound, the design logic shifts entirely. A harsh overhead rig — profile lanterns angled steeply downward, producing sharp shadows — communicates institutional control without a single piece of dialogue. Hanako is surveilled; the light does not flatter or warm, it locates and exposes.

The “searchlight” image referred to in the play’s design history extends this logic: a tight lighting special that picks out a performer centre stage, surrounded by darkness, functions as both interrogation lighting and a visual metaphor for isolation. A gobo patterned with a window-frame or horizontal bars, projected across Hanako’s body, makes her captivity legible without any set-piece prison construction.

A common student error is to write: “I would use cold blue lighting for the North Korea scenes to show it is cold and unfriendly.” Examiners need much more than this. Specify: which lantern type (profile spots for hard-edged shadows; Fresnels for a softer, more diffused chill), what intensity (70% rather than full, so the actors are readable but the environment feels leached of warmth), what colour gel (a Lee 201 “Full C.T. Blue” or similar cold wash), and what directional angle (steep top-light creates institutional surveillance rather than the enveloping cold of a side or front wash). Each specific choice carries meaning; a generic description carries none.

Sound Design: Waves and Propaganda

The play’s soundscape moves between two very different audio environments. The Japan scenes carry the sound of the sea — waves that begin as natural beach noise and gradually, across the play, become something the family has to choose to hear or not. A sound designer might position the sea sound binaurally (from the sides of the auditorium) in early scenes, then bring it to a mono centre speaker in later scenes, as if the sea has retreated into memory.

The North Korean compound scenes can be underscored by institutional sound — a low, steady drone that belongs to the building, not to nature; or, more specifically, by occasional fragments of state propaganda broadcast — distant music, an announcer’s voice — that arrive not as dramatic set-pieces but as background texture, as ordinary as traffic. This is the sound of a system that does not need to shout because it is simply the air you breathe. A soundscape underscore of this kind is more unsettling than a dramatic sound cue precisely because it feels unremarkable.

Key Fact

The sea functions as a controlling sound motif: it begins the play (the beach storm where Hanako disappears) and it is always available to the sound designer as a marker of the original loss. In the North Korean scenes, the absence of the sea — or its replacement by state sound — measures how far Hanako has been taken from herself.

Set Design: Minimalism Across Decades

Because the play covers 24 years and two countries, a realistic naturalistic set would require constant scene changes and would slow the play’s momentum fatally. Turnly’s play calls for a minimalist set: a stage that holds both locations simultaneously, with a handful of key elements that can be rearranged or relit to signal transitions. A low platform levels structure can separate the domestic Japanese household at one depth from the clinical compound surfaces at another, without a scene change.

Projections on the cyclorama can carry the sea without requiring a physical construction: a rolling ocean image projected behind the Japan scenes gives way to a blank institutional wall in the North Korean compound sequences. This also allows the projection to evolve — the sea becoming stormier or calmer — in response to the emotional arc of the family’s scenes.

Costume: Decade, Culture, Coercion

Costume in The Great Wave carries enormous narrative load because it must show the passage of decades (1979 to 2003) and the erasure of Hanako’s Japanese identity within the North Korean state. The design must signal two things simultaneously: the historical period (1980s Japanese civilian clothing moves through decades) and the institutional pressure on identity (Hanako’s costume in North Korea becoming less her own over time — more muted, more uniform, less personal).

For the Japanese family scenes, costume colour and silhouette can reflect period fashion while also tracking emotional states: Etsuko’s palette might grow greyer as the years pass, her costume gradually losing the bright accent colours of the early scenes. For Hanako in captivity, a DPRK-inflected institutional grey or khaki — plain fabric, functional cut — replaces the personal clothing of the beach scene. The contrast between what she wore at 17 and what she wears a decade later can be read by the audience as the visual measure of what she has lost.

Design choices only work if the performer engages with them. A performer playing Hanako in the compound scenes can use proxemics to reinforce the costume’s meaning: keeping a formal, controlled distance from officials, never allowing her body to claim the space as her own — the body contained within the uniform rather than inhabiting it. When Hanako has a rare private moment, a small physical release — dropping the shoulders, letting the hands open — can signal the self that still exists underneath the institutional costume. These micro-choices are what separate a performance that merely wears the costume from one that lives in it.
exam_tip_html: For “How would you (as a designer) design” questions (8 marks), the single most penalised error is generic description: “I would use dark lighting to show North Korea is oppressive.” Examiners need: the specific lantern type (profile spot for hard-edged shadows), the gel colour (a cold Lee 201 blue or similar), the angle (steep overhead to create institutional surveillance), the intensity (70% to leach warmth without losing visibility), and the effect on the audience at a named moment (when Hanako first arrives in the compound, the harsh overhead light makes her look exposed and vulnerable, signalling to the audience that she has no protection here). The same discipline applies to sound: name the specific audio element (recorded wave sound binaural from side speakers) and the specific effect (the audience locates themselves at the Japanese coast immediately). Design questions reward precision — general ideas score at Developing; concrete named choices score at Mastering.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A split staging strategy differentiates Japan and North Korea without constant scene changes: contrasting lighting states (warm amber wash versus steep overhead profile spot with cold gel), distinct sound environments (sea soundscape versus institutional drone), and minimalist set elements that can be relit to shift location.
  • Specific design vocabulary is essential in exam answers: name the lantern type, gel colour, gobo pattern, fabric, and directional angle for every design choice — not just “cold blue lighting” but exactly which lantern, what gel, at what intensity, from what angle, and what effect on the audience at a named moment.
  • Costume tracks both historical period and identity erosion: Hanako’s clothing in North Korea becomes progressively more institutional over the decades, providing a visual measure of what the state has taken from her. Performers can reinforce costume meaning through proxemics and physical choices.

practice_questions.text: Name one staging configuration suitable for The Great Wave and explain one advantage it would offer for staging the play's two locations.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming a valid staging configuration (proscenium arch, thrust, end-on, in-the-round, traverse) with a brief explanation of its advantage for this play. Example: thrust — brings audience close to both worlds simultaneously, reducing comfortable distance from the injustice.

practice_questions.text: What is a lighting special in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a lighting special is a single focused lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it illuminates one specific area or performer against a darker surrounding stage, creating contrast and isolating the subject.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer might use a minimalist set and levels to represent both Japan and North Korea without scene changes. Refer to specific set choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of minimalist approach — few scenic elements, location created through light and performer action (1); specific use of levels — e.g. a platform for the Japanese household and a lower, clinical floor for the North Korean compound (1); effect of simultaneous visibility on audience — both worlds are always present, reinforcing the play's parallel structure (1); link to meaning — the audience is never allowed to forget either location, holding the injustice in view throughout (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design lighting for the scenes set in the North Korean compound in The Great Wave. Refer to specific lighting choices — including lantern type, colour, angle and intensity — and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a fully specified lighting design — e.g. profile spotlights rigged steeply overhead (creating institutional surveillance shadows), Lee 201 Full C.T. Blue gel at 70% intensity (leaching warmth without losing visibility), a gobo of window bars projected across Hanako’s body (making captivity legible without scenic construction), and the surrounding stage in near-darkness so the spotlight functions as a searchlight. Every choice is anchored to a named moment (e.g. the first interrogation, a teaching scene) and the effect on the audience is explicitly stated: the audience feels Hanako is exposed and without protection.

Secure: at least two specific choices (lantern type and colour, or angle and gobo); at least one named moment; effect on audience present.

Developing: general lighting ideas (“cold blue lighting,” “harsh spotlights”) without specifying lantern type, gel, angle or intensity; effect is implied rather than stated.

Emerging: describes the desired “mood” of the lighting without any specific technical choices; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Turnly's intentions in contrasting the physical environments of Japan and North Korea throughout The Great Wave. What does he want the audience to understand about the two worlds and the relationship between them?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: analyses multiple intentions — the contrast between natural and institutional environments communicates the violence done to Hanako by the state; the sea as a shared but impassable element in both worlds embodies the theme of separation; the domestic warmth of Japan against the surveillance logic of North Korea is a political argument about the cost of state authoritarianism on individual life. Specific dramatic methods (stage directions specifying the sea, the contrast between open coastal setting and enclosed compound) are linked to specific intended audience effects. The response shows awareness that Turnly’s play is rooted in the real DPRK abductions and that the design choices must honour that reality.

Secure: identifies the contrast between locations and links it to themes of captivity and family loss; generally accurate about intended effect; at least one reference to a specific dramatic method.

Developing: describes the two locations and notes they are different; limited analysis of intention; effect on audience implied.

Emerging: lists features of each location without explaining what Turnly intends the contrast to communicate.

practice_questions.text: You are designing the full production of The Great Wave. Discuss how you would use set, lighting, sound and costume to differentiate between the Japan and North Korea scenes and to communicate the passage of over twenty years. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a coherent design concept is proposed and applied across all four disciplines. Set: minimalist split stage, levels differentiating locations, cyclorama projection of sea for Japan and blank wall for compound. Lighting: warm amber wash for Japan versus steep overhead profile spots with cold gel and bar-gobo for North Korea; lighting state transitions signalling time. Sound: binaural wave soundscape for Japan, institutional drone and distant propaganda audio for compound, sea sound growing quieter over decades. Costume: period 1980s Japanese clothing for the family aging across decades versus Hanako’s costume becoming progressively more institutional in North Korea. All choices are specific (named gel, lantern type, fabric, silhouette), anchored to named moments, and linked to audience effect and directorial intention (the wave as controlling metaphor).

Secure: at least three design disciplines addressed with generally concrete choices; some named moments; effect on audience present.

Developing: general ideas across disciplines; few specific technical choices; limited sense of a coherent design concept.

Emerging: describes what each location “should look like” without specific design choices; no named moments; no discussion of audience effect.

knowledge_checks.q: What is split staging in theatre design?
options: A stage divided so two locations are visible simultaneously, separated by light or levels
A staging style where the audience sits on both sides of a long central stage
A technique where performers switch between two roles in the same scene
The use of a revolving stage to change between locations quickly

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of lantern produces a hard-edged beam of light, suitable for interrogation scenes in The Great Wave?
A _____ is a large curved or flat screen at the back of the stage, used for projected images or as a background for lighting.
Music or sound played quietly beneath dialogue to support the atmosphere without drawing attention is called a soundscape _____.
Match each design element to its purpose in The Great Wave:
right: Creates a surveillance feeling in the North Korean compound
Locates the Japan scenes and evokes the site of loss
Shows the erosion of Hanako's personal identity over decades

flashcard_questions.a: Two locations represented simultaneously on stage, separated by light or levels.
A single focused lantern that illuminates one performer or area against a darker stage.
A stage using as few scenic elements as possible, with light and sound creating location.

flashcard_questions.q: What lantern type creates hard-edged shadows suitable for interrogation lighting?

flashcard_questions.a: A large screen at the back of the stage for projected images or background lighting.

flashcard_questions.q: What is levels in set design?
flashcard_questions.a: The use of different heights — platforms, rostra, ramps — to create visual interest or signal status.

flashcard_questions.q: What sound design strategy could distinguish Japan from North Korea in The Great Wave?
flashcard_questions.a: Wave soundscape for Japan; institutional drone or propaganda audio for North Korea.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Hanako's costume in the North Korean compound scenes communicate over the decades?
flashcard_questions.a: The progressive erasure of her personal identity by the state.
Broad light covering the whole stage, used to create atmosphere rather than highlight individuals.

flashcard_questions.q: What design element could make Hanako's captivity visible without scenic construction?
flashcard_questions.a: A gobo projecting window-bar or grid patterns across her body.

flashcard_questions.q: What staging configuration brings the audience close to the action on three sides?

flashcard_questions.a: The physical and spatial relationship between performers, communicating status or emotion.

glossary_terms.definition: A staging approach where two distinct locations are represented simultaneously on stage, often separated by light or level.
The overall shape and configuration of a performance space: how stage and audience are arranged relative to each other.
A stage that extends into the audience on three sides, with spectators on three sides and the backstage on the fourth.
A broad wash of light covering the whole stage area, often used to create atmosphere or suggest an environment rather than illuminate specific actors.
A single focused lantern used to illuminate one specific area or performer, creating contrast against the darker surrounding stage.
A metal or glass plate placed in front of a lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage — used here to suggest a window frame, bars, or fragmented light.
A layered design of sound — recorded or live — that creates the atmosphere of a place or moment, using multiple audio elements simultaneously.
Music or sound played quietly beneath dialogue or action to support the emotional atmosphere without drawing attention to itself.
An approach to set design that uses as few pieces of furniture and scenery as possible, creating location through light, sound and performer action rather than literal construction.
The use of different heights on stage — platforms, rostra, ramps — to create visual interest, signal status, or differentiate locations.
A large curved or flat screen at the back of the stage, used for projected images or as a background for lighting.
The physical and spatial relationship between two performers on stage, used to communicate status, emotional connection, or threat.
